title: Kerala Bets on Early Detection to Prevent Child Deaths From Malnutrition, Neglect
excerpt: After a toddler's suspected malnutrition death in Alappuzha, the state's plan leans on anganwadi and ASHA networks, district protection units and Mission Vatsalya to flag at-risk children before neglect turns fatal.
body:
• Kerala's response rests on early identification: Anganwadi workers, ASHAs, teachers and health staff flag malnutrition, developmental delays and neglect during home visits and nutrition programmes.
  • The framework runs through 14 District Child Protection Units and 14 Child Welfare Committees under the Juvenile Justice Act and Mission Vatsalya, with cases referred via police, schools, hospitals or Child Helpline 1098.
  • The urgency is concrete: in Alappuzha this month a two-year-old weighing 7.6 kg, against an expected 12 kg, died in a suspected malnutrition case, prompting child rights commission proceedings.
  • Programmes such as KAVAL Plus and the Balasuraksha Protocol add psychosocial care, but crime data show prevention still lags response.

Kerala is trying to stop child deaths linked to malnutrition and neglect before they happen, by pushing detection into homes, anganwadis and schools rather than waiting for a hospital or police case. The Hindu's explainer on the state's plan comes after a series of deaths that exposed how children can fall through a system that, on paper, is among India's most complete.

The immediate trigger for renewed scrutiny came from Alappuzha. On October 19, the Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights registered a case over the death of a two-year-old boy in Haripad, in a suspected case of malnutrition, the Press Trust of India reported. The child was severely anaemic and weighed 7.6 kg, against an expected weight of around 12 kg for his age, police said. Commission member T.C. Jalaja Mol initiated proceedings based on media reports and sought explanations from the District Medical Officer, the Karthikappally gram panchayat secretary, the District Child Protection Officer and the panchayat's ICDS supervisor. The Child Welfare Committee has taken the surviving children into its care.

How early identification is supposed to work

According to an IMPRI analysis of Kerala's community-based child protection framework, early identification relies on the state's network of Anganwadi workers, ASHAs, teachers, healthcare professionals and social workers, whose routine contact through schools, health services, nutrition programmes and home visits lets them spot warning signs such as malnutrition, developmental delays, behavioural changes, domestic violence and caregiver substance abuse. The Women and Child Development Department is the nodal agency; District Child Protection Units coordinate with police, health and education departments, local self-governments and civil society to identify vulnerable children and run social investigations.

Child Welfare Committees, empowered under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, decide interventions — counselling, family restoration, foster care, institutional care or rehabilitation — based on those reports. Kerala has 14 District Child Protection Units and 14 Child Welfare Committees, one set per district, and Mission Vatsalya adds community Child Protection Committees under local self-governments to identify vulnerable households.

Beyond rescue: psychosocial support

Programmes such as Mission Vatsalya (2021), the Balasuraksha Protocol (2019) and KAVAL Plus (2024) have shifted the model from reactive response toward prevention and rehabilitation, the IMPRI analysis notes. KAVAL Plus provides psychosocial assessments, individual care plans, family counselling, educational support and mental healthcare for child survivors, with documented cases of children returning to school after coordinated intervention. On nutrition, Kerala's anganwadi system tracks growth through cards that monitor physical, cognitive and emotional development, and menus have been overhauled under schemes serving eggs and milk through anganwadis — even as NFHS-5 recorded stunting among Kerala children rising from 19.7% to 23.4%, a warning that strong health indicators coexist with persistent undernutrition.

Where the system still fails

The data explain the push for reform. Kerala Police statistics cited by IMPRI show cognisable crimes against children rose from 3,941 cases in 2020 to 5,537 in 2025, with 1,886 cases already reported between January and May 2026; cases under the POCSO Act rose from 1,243 in 2020 to 2,242 in 2025. In May 2026, 18-month-old Arshid from Nedumangad in Thiruvananthapuram died after prolonged abuse, in a case where investigators said warning signs were missed. A Comptroller and Auditor General report in 2025 flagged deficiencies in monitoring and inter-agency coordination.

For families, the practical route into the system is early and local: report suspected neglect to an Anganwadi worker, a school, or the Child Helpline at 1098, which can refer a case to the Child Welfare Committee. The state's bet is that more eyes, earlier, will close the gap between a framework that responds well after harm and one that prevents it.
